subject: maths
stem: How is the number 45,207 read?
rationale: The comma marks thousands: 45 thousand, then 2 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones, so forty-five thousand two hundred seven. C reads the 0 and 7 the wrong way round; D drops the hundreds.

subject: maths
stem: What is 6,782 rounded to the nearest hundred?
rationale: 6,782 lies between 6,700 and 6,800, and 82 is more than half of a hundred, so it rounds up to 6,800. Rounding down gives 6,700; rounding to the nearest thousand gives 7,000.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these numbers is the greatest?
rationale: Compare the ten thousands and thousands first: 39 thousand beats 38 thousand, leaving 39,018 and 39,009. Then the tens: 18 is more than 09, so 39,018 is greatest. 38,999 has the most 9s, which is the trap.

subject: maths
stem: Which fraction is equal to 1/2?
rationale: 3/6 is 3 pieces out of 6 equal pieces, which is half the whole, so 3/6 = 1/2. 1/4 is half of a half; 2/3 and 2/5 are not halves.

subject: maths
stem: Two chocolate bars are exactly the same size. Which is the bigger piece: 1/3 of one bar or 1/2 of the other?
rationale: With the same whole, fewer equal parts means bigger parts: a half is bigger than a third. "It cannot be told" is right only when the bars differ in size, which is the point the chapter makes.

subject: maths
stem: A quarter turn makes
rationale: A quarter turn is a right angle, like the corner of a page. Two quarter turns make a straight angle and four make a full turn; an acute angle is less than a quarter turn.

subject: maths
stem: How many quarter turns make one full turn?
rationale: Four quarter turns in the same direction bring you back to where you started, which is a full turn. Two quarter turns make only a half turn.

subject: maths
rationale: Add by place value: ones 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 and carry 1; tens 2 + 4 + 1 = 7; hundreds 3 + 1 = 4; thousands 4 + 2 = 6. So 6,473. Forgetting the carry gives 6,463.

subject: maths
stem: How many centimetres are there in 3 metres?
rationale: 1 m = 100 cm, so 3 m = 3 × 100 = 300 cm. Using 10 (millimetres in a centimetre) gives 30; using 1,000 (metres in a kilometre) gives 3,000.

subject: maths
stem: Vijay rounded a number to the nearest thousand and got 5,000. Which of these could his number have been?
rationale: 4,780 is nearer 5,000 than 4,000, so it rounds to 5,000. 4,420 rounds to 4,000, and 5,620 and 5,500 round up to 6,000. 5,500 is the trap: being "5-something" does not make it round to 5,000.

subject: maths
stem: Without adding them one by one, find 49 + 50 + 51.
rationale: Three consecutive numbers add up to three times the middle one: 3 × 50 = 150, because 49 is one less than 50 and 51 one more. Adding gives the same, 150.

subject: maths
stem: A ribbon is 2 m 35 cm long. What is its length in centimetres?
rationale: 2 m = 200 cm, and 200 + 35 = 235 cm. Writing 2 m 35 cm as 37 or 2,035 are the usual slips.

subject: maths
stem: Meena ate 2/8 of a pizza. Arjun ate 1/4 of another pizza of the same size. Who ate more?
rationale: 2/8 is 2 of 8 equal slices; joining slices in pairs makes 1 of 4 equal parts, so 2/8 = 1/4 and they ate the same. Meena looks bigger because 2 and 8 are bigger numbers, which is the trap.

subject: maths
stem: Along one straight road from a city, town A is 1,855 km away and town B is 2,310 km away, further on. How far is town B from town A, in km?
rationale: Both are measured from the city along the same road, so the distance between them is the difference: 2,310 − 1,855 = 455 km. Adding them, 4,165 km, is the trap.

subject: maths
stem: A clock's minute hand points at 12. It turns clockwise through three quarter turns. Which number does it point at now?
rationale: Each quarter turn clockwise moves the hand on by three numbers: 12 to 3, 3 to 6, 6 to 9. Turning anti-clockwise by mistake ends at 3; one quarter turn alone ends at 3 as well.

subject: science
stem: When water is cooled enough in a freezer, it turns into
rationale: Water has three forms: liquid, solid (ice) and vapour (as in steam). Cooling turns it into ice; heating, not cooling, makes steam.

subject: science
stem: Which of these holds salty water?
rationale: Sea water is salt water. Wells, rivers and ponds hold fresh water, which people, animals and plants depend on.

subject: science
stem: If all the water on Earth were in one glass, about how much of it would be fresh water?
rationale: Almost all of Earth's water is salty sea water; the fresh water would fill only about a teaspoon, which is why it must be used wisely.

subject: science
stem: In the water cycle, the Sun's heat turns water from seas and rivers into
rationale: Heat turns water into water vapour, which rises, cools into droplets and falls back as rain. Ice comes from cooling, not heating; salt is left behind in the sea.

subject: science
stem: Smaller streams and rivers that join a big river are called its
rationale: Streams that join a river and make it bigger are its tributaries. A delta is where it spreads out at the sea, and a dam and reservoir hold its water back.

subject: science
stem: A river that flows all year round is called a ___ river.
rationale: A perennial river flows all year round, like the Godavari. A seasonal river flows only when the rains fill it.

subject: science
stem: The large body of water stored behind a dam is called a
rationale: A dam is like a giant wall across a river, and the water it holds back is the reservoir. A delta is at the river's mouth, and a glacier is ice.

subject: science
stem: The tiny living things that grow on food and spoil it are called
rationale: Microbes are living things too small to see one by one; they grow on food and change it. Mould is a colony of thousands of them. Some microbes are useful, as in making curd.

subject: science
stem: Chillies are dried in the Sun mainly so that they
rationale: Drying takes the moisture out, and without moisture microbes cannot grow, so the chillies keep for months. Drying makes them lighter, not heavier.

subject: science
stem: Microbes need moisture, air and the right temperature to grow. Drying food in the Sun stops them mainly by taking away
rationale: Drying removes water, the moisture microbes need. Dried food is still in the air and the light, so A and C are not what drying changes.

subject: science
stem: Where a river reaches the sea and spreads out into many small streams, it forms a
rationale: Near the sea a river splits into many small streams and the land between them is its delta. Tributaries join a river higher up; the source is where it begins.

subject: science
stem: A closed plastic bag with some water in it is kept in the Sun. Drops of water form on the inside of the bag. They form because the water vapour
rationale: The Sun turns some water into vapour; when the vapour touches the cooler bag it cools and turns back into droplets, the same way clouds form. It does not turn to ice in the Sun.

subject: science
stem: Pickles covered with a layer of oil stay good for months. The oil helps mainly by

options.B: keeping air away from the food

rationale: Microbes need air to grow, and oil on top seals the pickle off from the air. Adding moisture would help microbes, the opposite of what is wanted.

subject: science
stem: Why does a river flow from the mountains down to the sea and never the other way?

options.A: Water flows from higher to lower ground
options.B: The sea pulls the river water towards it
options.C: The wind blows the water along the land
options.D: Fish swim along and push the water

rationale: Water always flows downhill, from higher ground to lower ground, following the shape of the land; mountains are high and the sea is low. The other options are not what moves a river.

subject: science
stem: Butter spoils outside a fridge, but ghee, made by heating butter until its water is gone, keeps for months. Why does ghee keep longer?

options.B: Ghee has more salt in it
options.C: Ghee has no water for microbes

rationale: Heating drives the water out of butter to make ghee, and without moisture microbes cannot grow. Ghee is not sweeter or saltier than butter.
